question:
[MCQ] Based on the clip, what imaging adjustment is being made, and why?
A. Adjust overall gain/TGC to reduce near-field clutter and improve contrast of the target without changing depth
B. Decrease depth and set the focal region near the surface to better image a superficial target
C. Increase depth and move the focal zone deeper to better visualize a deep structure in the far field
D. Switch to a lower-frequency curvilinear transducer to improve penetration when the target is too deep for a linear probe
groundtruth: Depth and focus are adjusted for near-field imaging because the tendon is a very superficial structure and requires superficial-focused settings for optimal visualization.
original_question:
[MCQ] Based on the clip, what imaging adjustment is being made, and why?

B. Increase depth and move the focal zone deeper to better visualize a deep structure in the far field
C. Adjust overall gain/TGC to reduce near-field clutter and improve contrast of the target without changing depth
D. Switch to a lower-frequency curvilinear transducer to improve penetration when the target is too deep for a linear probe

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
Explanation: The depth marker remains fixed at 2.2 cm for the full duration of the clip, eliminating options B and C that involve changing depth, and no transducer switch is observed to rule out D. The visible changes to image contrast and reduction of near-field clutter are consistent with gain/TGC adjustment while depth is unchanged, to improve visualization of the target structure.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the video, what probe motion strategy is being used, and what is the objective?
A. Slide along the long axis to track the structure from its distal attachment toward where muscle fibers begin
B. Rotate to a short-axis view and sweep proximally to assess tendon thickness and surrounding sheath for tenosynovitis.
C. Use a heel-toe/rocking motion at the enthesis to center the cortical interface and look for cortical irregularity or enthesophytes.
D. Fan/tilt in the long axis to maintain perpendicular insonation and minimize anisotropy while optimizing tendon echogenicity at the attachment.
groundtruth: With the scanning hand anchored, the probe is slid proximally to follow the tendon’s length from the calcaneus up to the musculotendinous junction where muscle fibers begin.

C. Rotate to a short-axis view and sweep proximally to assess tendon thickness and surrounding sheath for tenosynovitis.
D. Slide along the long axis to track the structure from its distal attachment toward where muscle fibers begin

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: A
The probe is observed sliding linearly along the long axis of the imaged structure, starting at the bright, curved bony distal attachment site, then moving proximally to visualize the transition to the soft tissue where muscle fibers begin, matching the description in option A. Other motions (rotation, heel-toe rocking, fanning/tilting) described in the remaining options are not observed in the video.

question:
[MCQ] Based on the clip, what maneuver is performed at the transition zone and what is the purpose?
A. Apply color Doppler at the transition zone to confirm the structure is vascular before proceeding with measurements.
B. Use a heel-toe (rocking) maneuver at the transition zone to minimize anisotropy and optimize tendon/nerve echogenicity.
C. Fan/tilt the probe to maintain the long-axis view through the transition zone for a continuous assessment of echotexture.
D. Rotate the probe ~90° to obtain an orthogonal (cross-sectional) view and then track the structure back distally
groundtruth: After reaching the musculotendinous junction, the probe is rotated 90 degrees into transverse orientation and then slid distally to follow the tendon in short axis.

inference_metadata.raw_response:
Answer: D
First, no color Doppler is seen in the clip, eliminating option A. The view changes completely from a long-axis linear layered appearance to a cross-sectional/short axis appearance, which is consistent with ~90 degree probe rotation to get an orthogonal view, rather than heel-toe rocking (B) or fanning to maintain long axis (C). The orange dot then tracks the structure in this new cross-sectional view, matching option D.
